pacing.review: Narada answers Valmiki’s search for an exemplary person.
The brief whole-life outline is explicitly a prologue, not a jump in the main journey.
The bird’s death and its mate’s grief motivate the first verse; fallen bird visible, no gore.
Brahma’s encouragement leads to meditation and composition.
Teaching leads to Lava/Kusha’s later court performance; later-time label prevents age confusion.
Return from the prologue to Dasharatha’s prosperous Ayodhya.
Counsel establishes the king and Vashishtha before the succession concern.
Concern for an heir motivates the rite and Sumantra’s invitation proposal.
Anga’s drought establishes why Romapada sought Rishyasringa; explicit earlier-story framing.
Women act as city envoys, not Dasharatha’s queens; gifts motivate friendship.
The sage seeks the visitors and accompanies them to Anga.
Arrival resolves the drought and leads to honour and Shanta’s marriage.
Dasharatha visits Anga before the couple travels to Ayodhya; invitation order visible.
Preparations and completed Ashvamedha precede the separate Putreshti.
Putreshti and the gods’ concern introduce the parallel divine strand.
Ravana’s unprotected human vulnerability motivates Vishnu’s resolve.
The divine messenger gives payasa; Sumitra’s two shares retained.
The future vanara helpers prepare the wider arc, before the princes’ births.
Three mothers and four infants clearly identified in both copy and art.
Time advances to study; both brother-pair bonds retained.
Adolescence and elder Vishwamitra’s arrival establish the audience.
Dasharatha’s existing question now has a dedicated close-up and protected speech area.
The disrupted sacrifice gives Vishwamitra a concrete reason to request Rama.
Dasharatha’s fear motivates his offer to go instead; under-sixteen claim remains contextual.
Vishwamitra’s displeasure and Vashishtha’s counsel answer the refusal.
Acceptance, blessing and departure conclude the court exchange.
Departure leads to the first riverbank lesson in Bala and Atibala.
River-confluence welcome introduces the narrated Kamadeva history; current trio remains visible.
Rama’s roar question now receives the Sarayu–Ganga answer before entry into Tataka’s region.
Tataka’s family and curse establish the danger and connect Maricha to the next conflict.
Rama’s initial restraint and the sage’s protective-duty answer precede combat.
Sound of the bow provokes the dust-and-stone attack; both brothers respond.
Replaced ambiguous aftermath with Tataka’s visible fall at dusk; death explicit in both languages.
Added night rest closes the confrontation and motivates the next morning’s lesson.
Next morning is explicit after the night-rest panel; Rama receives the divine weapons.
Rama asks how to recall the weapons; instruction completes the restraint lesson.
Added resumed walk, pleasant grove and Rama’s hermitage question before the flashback.
Vishwamitra’s answer introduces Vamana/Bali as the place’s ancient story, not a present event.
Explicit return to the travelling trio and arrival at Siddhashrama leads to guarding the rite.
Six days and nights of watch establish the obligation and passing time.
Final-day attack; Maricha is hurled away but explicitly survives.
Subahu’s continued attack ends in death; fallen body visible, distinct from Maricha.
Uninterrupted completion and praise resolve the task before the Mithila invitation.
Successful protection leads to the sages’ Mithila journey and interest in Shiva’s bow.
Rest beside Shona frames Vishwamitra’s family retrospective.
The daughters refuse the proposal; Vayu’s retaliation is identified as injustice, not blame on them.
The daughters report the event and receive their father’s support.
Marriage to Brahmadatta resolves their altered condition in the narrated tradition.
Gadhi/Satyavati/Kaushiki connect the family account back to present narrator Vishwamitra.
Rama’s Ganga question motivates the divine family story.
Ganga and Uma’s different paths lead to Agni bearing the divine energy.
Agni/Ganga lead to Sharavana and Kumara’s birth; six foster mothers retained.
Six-faced Kartikeya’s appointment completes the birth-and-role arc.
Sagara’s family and Asamanjasa’s exile establish the genealogy and motive.
The stolen horse prevents completion of the rite and triggers the search.
Destructive digging leads the sons to Kapila rather than an unexplained confrontation.
Mistaking Kapila for the thief causes the attack and reduction to ashes.
The missing sons prompt Anshuman’s search; ashes and horse make the consequence visible.
Garuda explains the need for Ganga; returning the horse closes the immediate rite.
Several generations pass; Bhagiratha inherits the unresolved task.
Austerities win Brahma’s response, which establishes why Shiva is needed.
Shiva’s favour enables the descent and restrains Ganga’s force.
Further prayer releases seven streams; one follows Bhagiratha.
Flooding Jahnu’s rite causes the interruption; wave image is symbolic, not literal drinking.
The gods’ appeal restores the flow and explains the name Jahnavi.
Water reaches the ashes and completes the ancestors’ deliverance.
Praise and the narrator’s conclusion return to Rama’s travelling party.
Near Vishala, Vishwamitra explicitly opens the ancient churning account.
Mandara/Vasuki and the sinking mountain motivate Vishnu’s tortoise support.
Poison threatens the worlds; Shiva’s intervention averts the danger.
The treasures and nectar appear, leading to a dispute.
Vishnu’s help and the gods’ victory lead into Diti’s grief in the next episode.
Loss of sons motivates Diti’s wish and Kashyapa’s prescribed vow.
Indra’s fear and the lapse lead to seven parts; represented symbolically, without bodily harm imagery.
Diti’s request and Indra’s acceptance resolve the conflict as the Maruts.
The ancient account returns to the present welcome by King Sumati in Vishala.
The deserted hermitage motivates Rama’s question and the Gautama/Ahalya retrospective.
Indra’s disguise, recognition and Gautama’s return explain the curse; not a stone version.
Unseen penance and the stated condition for its end establish the long wait.
Rama/Lakshmana’s arrival fulfils the condition; mutual honour and hospitality visible.
Gautama’s reunion and blessing close the arc before departure for Mithila.
Arrival in Mithila follows Ahalya’s hermitage; Janaka hears the princes’ accomplishments.
Shatananda’s relationship to Ahalya motivates his question about her reception.
His response introduces Vishwamitra’s earlier king-to-sage life as a framed retrospective.
Royal Vishwamitra’s arrival and Shabala’s hospitality establish the desired power.
The offer and Vashishtha’s refusal explain why the cow cannot be taken.
Force prompts Shabala’s appeal and permission to defend herself.
Defeat and loss of sons motivate Vishwamitra’s grief and revenge; aftermath rather than battle detail.
Austerities obtain weapons from Shiva; the caption establishes return to attack.
Vashishtha’s staff neutralizes the weapons and changes Vishwamitra’s understanding.
Renunciation and the Brahmarshi goal carry into further austerity.
Raj arshi recognition and Trishanku’s separate request introduce the next test.
Refusal, appeal to the sons and curse explain loss of royal splendour, without skin-tone caricature.
Trishanku seeks Vishwamitra’s refuge; the promise motivates the rite.
Invitations and refusals reveal Vishwamitra’s unresolved anger.
Ascent and rejection cause the headfirst fall and plea for protection.
The halted fall, new stars and agreement resolve Trishanku’s position.
Loss of the sacrificial animal causes a demand that endangers a boy, not an unexplained voluntary offering.
Family discussion leads to Shunahshepa accompanying the king; his fear remains explicit.
The boy actively seeks his relative’s protection at Pushkara.
Refusal by the sage’s sons precedes teaching protective prayers.
Recitation leads to long life and rescue; the boy is not killed.
Menaka interrupts austerity; years pass before the realization.
Peaceful parting and renewed effort distinguish this from the later angry response.
Rambha’s curse exposes the remaining failure to control anger.
Recognition of that failure motivates silence and patience.
Giving away the meal without anger demonstrates the changed response.
Brahma and Vashishtha’s recognition resolves the retrospective and cues Shiva’s bow.
Explicit return to present Mithila; family-held Shiva bow establishes the object.
Janaka’s remembered discovery and upbringing explain Sita’s origin.
His marriage condition and earlier failed kings explain the stakes, without adding Ravana to the scene.
Vishwamitra’s permission precedes Rama’s handling of the bow.
Lifting/stringing and the break cause the court’s astonishment; broken bow visible.
Janaka’s proposal and messengers lead directly to the invitation episode.
Messengers carry both the bow news and the princes’ well-being to Ayodhya.
Consultation and consent motivate Dasharatha’s journey with the other sons.
Welcome and reunion precede the marriage arrangements.
Kushadhvaja’s arrival and the Ikshvaku lineage identify both households.
Janaka’s lineage leads to the Rama/Sita and Lakshmana/Urmila proposals.
Kushadhvaja’s daughters are paired with Bharata/Shatrughna, not Janaka’s daughters.
Agreement leads to a chosen time, preparatory rites and gifts.
Yudhajit’s arrival explains his later role accompanying Bharata and Shatrughna.
Rama/Sita’s hand-taking at the sacred fire; Janaka’s adapted words retain companionship in dharma.
Lakshmana/Urmila marriage separately identified in green.
Bharata/Mandavi marriage separately identified in maroon.
Shatrughna/Shrutakirti marriage separately identified in blue.
All four couples and blessings close the wedding sequence before departure.
Next-morning farewell removes elder Vishwamitra from the returning party.
Storm and Parashurama’s arrival interrupt the return journey.
Two distinct bows are explained; the Vaishnava bow is not the broken Shiva bow.
Dasharatha’s plea and Parashurama’s direct challenge establish the conflict.
The bow is handed over and the task is stated before Rama’s response.
Rama’s prior silence and respectful response answer the challenge.
Stringing the Vaishnava bow demonstrates his strength and changes Parashurama’s response.
Rama refrains from bodily harm; two alternatives and Parashurama’s choice are explicit.
Release, acknowledgement and departure to Mahendra resolve the encounter.
The unbroken Vaishnava bow is entrusted to Varuna; travel resumes.
Homecoming shows the three mothers welcoming the four brides.
A later departure with Yudhajit distinguishes the maternal-family visit from the wedding return.
Service and Rama/Sita’s deepening affection close Bālakāṇḍa; exile/coronation not appended.
